domain_restrictions: A,B,d are integers with A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0
Empty product convention: if d=0 then ∏_{i=1}^0 (...) = 1 so Q_{A,B,0}(q)=1
Assumption: the rational expression Q_{A,B,d}(q) is actually a polynomial, i.e., Q_{A,B,d}(q) ∈ Q[q] (not just a rational function)
Graded ring S is Q[x_1,...,x_d] with weighted grading deg(x_i)=B+i for i=1..d
If d=0, interpret S as Q (no variables, hence no f_i witnesses needed)
Each f_i is homogeneous in S with weighted degree deg(f_i)=A+i
Regularity condition: in the successive quotient S/(f_1,...,f_{i-1}), the class of f_i is not a zero-divisor (equivalently: (f_1,...,f_d) is a homogeneous regular sequence in S)
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: Let A,B,d ∈ Z with A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0, and define Q_{A,B,d}(q)=∏_{i=1}^d (1-q^{A+i})/(1-q^{B+i}) with Q_{A,B,0}(q)=1. If Q_{A,B,d}(q) ∈ Q[q], then in the weighted graded polynomial ring S=Q[x_1,...,x_d] (or S=Q if d=0) with deg(x_i)=B+i, there exist homogeneous elements f_1,...,f_d ∈ S such that deg(f_i)=A+i for each i=1..d and for each i the class of f_i in S/(f_1,...,f_{i-1}) is not a zero-divisor (so f_1,...,f_d form a homogeneous regular sequence). Consequently, the graded data of S modulo this regular sequence yields the given expression Q_{A,B,d}(q) (as stated in the equivalence).

Assume Q_{A,B,d}(q) := ∏_{i=1}^d (1-q^{A+i})/(1-q^{B+i}) belongs to Q[q] (q formal indeterminate)
There exist homogeneous polynomials f_1, ..., f_d in S such that for each i=1..d: deg(f_i)=A+i, and the image of f_i in S/(f_1,...,f_{i-1}) is not a zero-divisor

ancestry_summary.statement_nl: For integers A, B, d with A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0, define Q_{A,B,d}(q) := prod_{i=1}^d (1 - q^(A+i)) / (1 - q^(B+i)), with the empty product equal to 1 when d = 0. Assume Q_{A,B,d}(q) belongs to Q[q]. Let S be the weighted polynomial ring Q[x_1, ..., x_d] graded by deg(x_i) = B+i; when d = 0 interpret S as Q. Then there exist homogeneous polynomials f_1, ..., f_d in S such that deg(f_i) = A+i for every i, and for each i the image of f_i in S/(f_1, ..., f_{i-1}) is not a zero-divisor. Equivalently, Q_{A,B,d}(q) is realized by a homogeneous regular sequence in a weighted polynomial ring with variable weights B+1, ..., B+d and relation degrees A+1, ..., A+d.

ancestry_summary.statement_nl: Let [n choose k]_q denote the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient. Prove that for all integers n, k, l with 0 ≤ k, l ≤ n, if [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q is a polynomial in q, then that polynomial has only nonnegative coefficients.

payload.proof_nl:
Let K be an algebraic closure of k, and set J := I K[x_1,...,x_d] inside K[x_1,...,x_d]. The weighted grading and the homogeneity of I are not needed for the argument.

First handle the case d = 0. Then S = k. The affine 0-space over K has exactly one point, namely the origin. If I = S, then its zero locus is empty, contrary to the hypothesis that the zero locus is exactly the origin. Hence I = 0, so S/I is isomorphic to k, which is finite-dimensional over k.

Now assume d >= 1. The common zero locus of J in K^d is the same as the common zero locus of I in K^d: every element of I lies in J, and every element of J is a finite K[x_1,...,x_d]-linear combination of elements of I, so a point of K^d annihilates all elements of I if and only if it annihilates all elements of J. By hypothesis, V(J) = {0}.

Because K is algebraically closed, Hilbert's Nullstellensatz gives that the radical of J is the ideal of all polynomials vanishing on V(J). Since V(J) = {0}, this ideal is exactly (x_1,...,x_d). Therefore, for each i = 1,...,d, we have x_i in rad(J), so there exists an integer N_i >= 1 such that x_i^(N_i) belongs to J.

We next prove that J intersect S = I. The inclusion I subseteq J intersect S is immediate. For the reverse inclusion, let f be an element of J intersect S. Since f belongs to J, there exist finitely many elements g_1,...,g_m of I and polynomials A_1,...,A_m in K[x_1,...,x_d] such that
f = sum_{r=1}^m A_r g_r.
Let V be the finite-dimensional k-subspace of K spanned by 1 and by all coefficients of all the A_r. Choose a k-basis b_1,...,b_t of V with b_1 = 1. Since every coefficient of each A_r lies in V, we can write uniquely
A_r = sum_{s=1}^t b_s B_{r,s}
with B_{r,s} in S = k[x_1,...,x_d]. Hence
f = sum_{s=1}^t b_s G_s,
where G_s := sum_{r=1}^m B_{r,s} g_r belongs to I for each s.
Now set H_1 := G_1 - f and H_s := G_s for s > 1. Then each H_s lies in S, and
sum_{s=1}^t b_s H_s = 0
in K[x_1,...,x_d]. Write each H_s as a finite sum
H_s = sum_alpha c_{s,alpha} x^alpha
with c_{s,alpha} in k. Since the monomials x^alpha are linearly independent over K in the polynomial ring K[x_1,...,x_d], for each multi-index alpha we get
sum_{s=1}^t b_s c_{s,alpha} = 0
in K. But b_1,...,b_t are k-linearly independent, and each c_{s,alpha} lies in k. Therefore all c_{s,alpha} are zero. So every H_s is the zero polynomial. In particular H_1 = 0, hence f = G_1 belongs to I. This proves J intersect S = I.

Applying this to x_i^(N_i), we obtain x_i^(N_i) in I for every i. Therefore any monomial x_1^(a_1) ... x_d^(a_d) with some a_i >= N_i lies in I, because it is divisible by x_i^(N_i). It follows that the residue classes of the finitely many monomials x_1^(a_1) ... x_d^(a_d) with 0 <= a_i < N_i for all i span S/I over k. Hence S/I is finite-dimensional as a k-vector space.

Thus the lemma is proved.

payload.statement_nl: Let k be a field, let d be a nonnegative integer, let w_1,...,w_d be positive integers, and let S = k[x_1,...,x_d] with weighted grading deg(x_i)=w_i. Let I be a homogeneous ideal of S. If, over an algebraic closure of k, the common zero locus of I in affine d-space is exactly the origin, then S/I is finite-dimensional as a k-vector space.

detailed_findings.finding: The core argument is sound: V(J)={0} implies rad(J)=(x_1,...,x_d), hence powers x_i^{N_i} lie in J; after proving J ∩ S = I, finitely many bounded monomials span S/I.
The contraction step J ∩ S = I is proved carefully and correctly by expanding coefficients in a finite k-basis of the coefficient space and using k-linear independence.

result_payload.reason: The proof is mathematically complete and matches the lemma: after extending scalars to an algebraic closure, it uses Nullstellensatz to deduce x_i^{N_i} ∈ J for each coordinate, proves the contraction identity J ∩ S = I by an explicit coefficient-separation argument, and then concludes that only finitely many monomial classes are needed to span S/I. There is no substantive semantic drift; in fact the argument proves a slightly stronger statement since the weighted grading/homogeneity is unused. However, the proof explicitly invokes Hilbert's Nullstellensatz even though no citation was declared and no such dependency appears in the allowed manifest, so the safest routing is to request a dependency-cleaned resubmission.
